title: Doug Ford encourages Ontarians to 'fight back' against home invasions
summary: The premier says he owns a gun and would not hesitate to use it on someone trying to break into his home, advising people without guns to use knives or baseball bats to protect themselves and their…

image.caption: Ontario Premier Doug Ford says he owns a gun and would not hesitate to use it on someone trying to break into his home, advising people to 'fight back' against intruders. (Evan Mitsui/CBC)

blocks.text: Toronto·Updated

The premier says he owns a gun and would not hesitate to use it on someone trying to break into his home, advising people without guns to use knives or baseball bats to protect themselves and their children.
Premier says he owns a gun and would not hesitate to use it on someone trying to break into his home
· The Canadian Press
· Posted: Nov 26, 2026 2:14 PM EST | Last Updated: 4 minutes ago
Ontario Premier Doug Ford says he wants to see legal changes to address a spate of home invasions, and in the meantime is advising people to "use anything you can to protect your family."

Ford says he is a legal gun owner and wouldn't hesitate to use it on someone trying to break into his home, advising people without guns to use knives or baseball bats to protect themselves and their children.
"I encourage people to use whatever tool they have to fight back," Ford told reporters at Queen's Park on Thursday. "Not hide, but fight back."
"Someone comes through my door with a gun and a knife and starts shooting it up, I'll blow the guy right through the front door. You'll look like Swiss cheese by the time he's done."

blocks.text: The premier was reacting to the fatal shooting of a 39-year-old musician during an overnight home invasion in an affluent midtown Toronto neighbourhood on Wednesday.
It happened nearly a month after a violent home invasion and shooting in the Bridle Path neighbourhood left a family of four adults injured.
Victim in fatal home invasion was Toronto musician
Police suggest contacting 911 first
Toronto police said in a Wednesday news conference that people facing home intruders should contact 911 first.

"The Toronto Police Service provides the very best that it can in terms of public safety services," said Det. Sgt. Alan Bartlett. "I would encourage people to contact 911 to tell people what is happening."
Green Party Leader Mike Schreiner said he trusts police.
"I would call 911 and make sure my family is safe and allow the police to do their job," he said. "I think it's incredibly dangerous to suggest to people that they should be shooting other people."

blocks.text: NDP Leader Marit Stiles said Ford should be looking for ways to ensure people feel safe in their own homes, not telling them to arm themselves in order to protect their families.
"Doug Ford, he's really good at writing letters and coming out with outrageous statements, but the truth is that he can control some things in the province of Ontario," she said.

blocks.text: "For example, we have absolutely overloaded courts right now in the province of Ontario. We are letting the bad guys out too soon because of these packed courts, and he can do something about that and refuses to take responsibility.
"He has the power as the premier of Ontario to be able to protect Ontarians, and instead he's saying, 'You're all on your own. Protect yourselves.' That is unacceptable."
Past comments on Ford's take on crime
It's not the first time the premier has advocated for a violent approach to crime.

At an unrelated news conference in June of last year, Ford told a story about masked men who had tried to steal a vehicle overnight from his home, saying that if they came back, he would "take care" of them better than the police.
At the same news conference, he said a man charged by York Regional Police for allegedly shooting a gun in the air during an attempted vehicle theft deserved a medal.

blocks.text: A few months later, the premier spoke about threatening to beat up a Home Depot shoplifter.
Earlier this year, he said a York Region resident who shot and injured an alleged home invader "should have shot him a couple more times."
"Congratulations," he said. "I'm glad you shot the guy."
Ontario Premier Doug Ford praises homeowner who shot intruder
Premier calls for legal change on federal level
Ford says he is directing his attorney general and solicitor general to look at legal changes that could bring the province "right up to the edge" of so-called castle law.

Ford has previously mused about introducing the castle doctrine, laws in some U.S. states that allow people to use reasonable force, sometimes including lethal force, to protect themselves in their homes.

items: Ford government's public safety efforts seen as 'largely ineffective,' internal polling reveals

blocks.text: Attorney General Doug Downey says there are already rules around self defence, but that they will examine whether the line is in the right spot.
Ford also called on the federal government to strengthen bail laws and increase mandatory jail time for violent offenders, which federal Conservative Leader Pierre Poilievre echoed.
"This unfortunately has become an all-too-common story," he said in Ottawa. "Canadians are literally afraid to go to sleep at night."

The federal government's Bail and Sentencing Reform Act, or Bill C-14, received royal assent in June. It makes over 80 changes to the Criminal Code, Youth Criminal Justice Act and the National Defence Act to make bail and sentencing laws tougher for repeat and violent offenders.

Meanwhile, criminal lawyers and justice advocates have said that the changes could put more pressure on an already backlogged court system while doing little to address the factors that lead people to commit crimes.

blocks.text: Home invasions hit a 10-year high in 2024, before dropping in 2025 and then rising again at the beginning of this year in Toronto, according to CBC News analysis of Toronto police data. Affluent areas with large detached houses and driveways were among the hardest hit.
